## Zephaniah 1 – Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1 – The Superscription: Prophet and Times

- **"The word of the LORD that came to Zephaniah"** – The Hebrew expression "word of the LORD" (דְּבַר־יְהוָה) is the standard prophetic formula emphasising divine authority: the message originates with God, not the prophet (Precept Austin). Zephaniah is a messenger, not the originator (enduringword.com; preceptaustin.org).
- **Zephaniah's name** means "Yahweh hides" or "Yahweh has hidden." He was likely born during Manasseh's wicked 55-year reign and hidden for his own protection (enduringword.com). Gill notes Jerome derived it as "the Lord's watch tower" or "his hidden one" (biblehub.com/gill).
- **Royal lineage**: Zephaniah traces his ancestry four generations back to **Hezekiah** (Hizkiah). Most conservative commentators—including Guzik, the KJV Bible Commentary, and Gill (citing Aben Ezra)—hold that this is the godly King Hezekiah, making Zephaniah of royal blood (enduringword.com; preceptaustin.org; biblehub.com/gill). Gill notes objections: the text doesn't say "king of Judah," and the generational timing is tight, but the consensus leans toward the royal identification (biblehub.com/gill).
- **"In the days of Josiah"** – Zephaniah prophesied during Josiah's reign (640–609 BC), likely before the great reform of 621 BC when the Book of the Law was found. MacArthur notes the moral and spiritual conditions described (vv. 4–6) suggest a date prior to Josiah's reforms, around 635–625 BC (preceptaustin.org). The prophecy probably helped spur the revival (enduringword.com). Gill discusses arguments for both earlier and later dating, noting the mention of "the remnant of Baal" suggests some reform had already occurred (biblehub.com/gill).
- Zephaniah was contemporary with Jeremiah, Nahum, and Habakkuk (preceptaustin.org).
- **Source URLs**: enduringword.com, preceptaustin.org, biblehub.com/gill

---

### vv. 2–3 – Universal Judgment Announced

- **"I will completely sweep away everything from the face of the earth"** – The Hebrew phrasing ("by taking away I will make an end") expresses certainty and totality. The Pulpit Commentary notes this recalls the judgment of the Flood (Genesis 6:7) (biblehub.com/pulpit, via search). Gill says "the land" refers specifically to the land of Judah, to be stripped bare by the Chaldeans/Babylonians (biblehub.com/gill).
- **"Man and beast… birds… fish"** – This reverses the creation order of Genesis 1. The judgment is comprehensive, touching every sphere of created life. Gill notes that fish were not destroyed in the Flood; here even they are included, whether literally or hyperbolically (biblehub.com/gill). The Pulpit Commentary sees this not as hyperbole but as reflecting the "mysterious connection between man and the lower creation" — creation suffers for man's sin (Romans 8:22) (biblehub.com/pulpit, via search).
- **"The idols with their wicked worshipers"** – Literally "the stumbling blocks." Gill identifies these as idols that cause men to stumble and fall. The Vulgate reads "the ruins of the wicked" (biblehub.com/gill). Precept Austin notes various English translations: "the rubble with the wicked" (ESV), "heaps of rubble" (NIV), reflecting a textual ambiguity — whether it refers to idols as stumbling blocks or to physical ruins (preceptaustin.org).
- **"I will cut off mankind"** – Repeated for emphasis. Guzik notes that Zephaniah "didn't waste any time getting to the point" — harsh and complete judgment (enduringword.com).
- **Near and far fulfillment**: Guzik and Precept Austin (citing Keathley) note an "oscillating prophecy" pattern — the near fulfillment was Babylon's destruction of Judah (586 BC), but the language also looks toward an eschatological, worldwide judgment at the end of the age (enduringword.com; preceptaustin.org). Chuck Smith likewise sees a "double aspect of fulfillment" — Babylon and the Great Tribulation (studylight.org/smith).
- **Source URLs**: enduringword.com, preceptaustin.org, biblehub.com/gill, studylight.org/smith

---

### v. 4 – Judgment Focuses on Judah and Jerusalem

- **"I will stretch out My hand against Judah"** – God now narrows the focus from universal judgment to His own covenant people. Guzik: "God would not allow them to think that He spoke just to others" (enduringword.com). The Pulpit Commentary notes that judgment begins at the house of God (1 Peter 4:17), because Judah's sin was more heinous — they had the temple, the services, and the priests and ought to have known better (biblehub.com/pulpit, via search). Gill: the hand stretched out is not for protection but for wrath — "dreadful and intolerable to bear" (biblehub.com/gill).
- **"Every remnant of Baal"** – The word "remnant" may imply Josiah's reforms had already begun removing Baal worship, or it may simply mean God will remove even the last trace. Guzik sees God's promise functioning as an invitation: "Baal and the idols are going to go. You can get rid of them in righteousness, or I will get rid of them in judgment" (enduringword.com).
- **"The idolatrous and pagan priests"** – The Hebrew *Chemarim* (black-robed ones) refers to idolatrous priests, also mentioned in 2 Kings 23:5 and Hosea 10:5. The Pulpit Commentary notes "the name is probably the Syriac name of 'priest,' used of idolatrous priests because the Syrians were idolaters." Gill suggests the name comes from black garments or smoke-blackened faces (biblehub.com/gill). The "priests" (*kohanim*) alongside them are the legitimate Levitical priests who had corrupted Yahweh's worship (biblehub.com/pulpit, via search).
- **Source URLs**: enduringword.com, biblehub.com/gill, preceptaustin.org

---

### v. 5 – Three Classes of False Worshippers (continued)

- **"Those who bow on the rooftops to worship the host of heaven"** – Astral worship (sun, moon, stars) was practiced on the flat roofs of houses, where altars were erected for burning incense and offering sacrifices (Jeremiah 19:13; 2 Kings 23:12). This was especially prevalent under Manasseh (2 Kings 21:3). The Pulpit Commentary notes that flat roofs were used for meditation, recreation, and sleeping in summer — making them convenient places for family star-worship (biblehub.com/pulpit, via search). Gill: worshippers fancied that the nearer they were to the heavenly bodies, the more acceptable their service (biblehub.com/gill).
- **"Those who bow down and swear by the LORD but also swear by Milcom"** – Syncretists: those who tried to blend Yahweh worship with pagan worship. "Milcom" (Malcham/Molech) was the god of the Ammonites. Gill calls them "occasional conformists" who "divided their religion and devotion between them" — as detestable to God as outright idolaters (biblehub.com/gill). The Pulpit Commentary calls them "waverers" who "halted between two opinions" (1 Kings 18:21) (biblehub.com/pulpit, via search). Gill applies this to all who seek justification partly by works and partly by Christ (biblehub.com/gill).
- **Source URLs**: biblehub.com/gill, enduringword.com

---

### v. 6 – Apostates and the Indifferent

- **"Those who turn back from following the LORD"** – Apostates who once followed Yahweh but have now abandoned Him. Gill suggests these may be those who renewed covenant in Josiah's time and then revolted (biblehub.com/gill).
- **"Neither seeking the LORD nor inquiring of Him"** – The religiously indifferent: practical atheists. Gill calls them "profane abandoned sinners, that lived without God in the world, and as if there was no God" (biblehub.com/gill). The Pulpit Commentary groups the worshippers of vv. 5–6 into three classes: open idolaters, syncretists, and those who despise religion altogether (biblehub.com/pulpit, via search). Precept Austin (citing Deffinbaugh) summarises: God judges pure pagans (v.4), mixers (v.5a), and complete rejecters (v.6) (preceptaustin.org).
- **Source URLs**: biblehub.com/gill, preceptaustin.org

---

### v. 7 – A Call to Silence; the Sacrifice Prepared

- **"Be silent in the presence of the Lord GOD"** – Literally "Hush!" Like Habakkuk 2:20. No disputing, no excuses — stand in awe. The Layman's Bible Commentary notes this may echo the liturgical call to silence before a ritual (studylight.org/lbc). Guzik: God tells the royalty to "shut up" and listen (enduringword.com). Precept Austin: "The Judge of all mankind is giving His verdict and you can hear a pin drop in the courtroom" (preceptaustin.org).
- **"The Day of the LORD is near"** – This is the central theme of Zephaniah (used 7 times in this chapter alone). Precept Austin notes the phrase appears more often in Zephaniah than in any other prophet. It has both a near historical fulfillment (Babylonian invasion) and an eschatological one (preceptaustin.org). Gill traces it beginning at Josiah's death, when "the Jews enjoyed little peace and prosperity" (biblehub.com/gill).
- **"The LORD has prepared a sacrifice; He has consecrated His guests"** – Shocking reversal of normal sacrificial imagery. The "sacrifice" is Judah itself, and the "consecrated guests" are the Babylonians (or Chaldeans), whom God has set apart as His instruments of judgment. Precept Austin: "Instead of a normal worship sacrifice, the 'sacrifice' is Judah itself, and the consecrated guests are the Babylonians" (preceptaustin.org). Peake's Commentary adds that the guests may also be the Scythians (studylight.org/peake). Gill notes Kimchi's suggestion that the "guests" also include the birds and beasts invited to feast on the slain (Ezekiel 39:17) (biblehub.com/gill). The Pulpit Commentary: the "called ones" are "sanctified" as if engaged in a holy war (biblehub.com/pulpit, via search).
- **Source URLs**: enduringword.com, preceptaustin.org, biblehub.com/gill, studylight.org/lbc, studylight.org/peake

---

### v. 8 – Judgment on Royalty and Foreign Adopters

- **"I will punish the princes, the sons of the king"** – Even the royal house is not exempt. Gill identifies these as the sons of Josiah: Jehoahaz (deposed by Egypt after 3 months), Jehoiakim (died in disgrace), and Jeconiah (carried captive to Babylon), or the sons of Zedekiah slain before his eyes (biblehub.com/gill). Guzik notes this warning came even to a godly king during a time of reform (enduringword.com).
- **"All who are dressed in foreign apparel"** – Those who adopted foreign (especially Assyrian or Babylonian) fashions, ashamed of their identity as God's people. Guzik: "They wanted to be as much like the worldly nations around them as they could possibly be" (enduringword.com). Gill offers multiple traditional interpretations: garments worn in honour of idols, hypocritical "holy" garments, cross-dressing, or simply imitating foreign fashions (biblehub.com/gill). The Targum renders it: "all those that make a noise at the worship of idols" (biblehub.com/gill).
- **Source URLs**: enduringword.com, biblehub.com/gill

---

### v. 9 – Judgment on Threshold-Leapers and the Violent

- **"All who leap over the threshold"** – This probably refers to a Philistine superstition: after Dagon fell on the threshold, the priests of Dagon would not tread on the threshold but leaped over it (1 Samuel 5:4-5). Gill says the Targum reads: "all those that walk in the laws of the Philistines" (biblehub.com/gill). Guzik sees it as "bringing pagan customs and superstitions into the house of God" (enduringword.com). Alternatively, it could refer to those who rushed violently into houses to plunder them (biblehub.com/gill, continued).
- **"Who fill the house of their master with violence and deceit"** – Servants or officials of the royal household who gained wealth through oppression and fraud. Bridgeway Commentary: "those who through corruption had won favour with the royal household" (studylight.org/bbc). The "master" may refer to the king or to Baal (if the house is a temple).
- **Source URLs**: enduringword.com, biblehub.com/gill, studylight.org/bbc

---

### vv. 10–11 – Judgment on Merchants: Cries Across Jerusalem

- **"A cry will go up from the Fish Gate"** – The Fish Gate was on the northern side of Jerusalem, likely where fish merchants brought their wares. Guzik notes merchants trusted in their riches — a form of idolatry (Colossians 3:5-6) (enduringword.com).
- **"A wail from the Second District"** – The "Second Quarter" (Mishneh) was a newer western suburb of Jerusalem (mentioned in 2 Kings 22:14). Cries spread from north to west.
- **"A loud crashing from the hills"** – Possibly the sound of buildings collapsing or the noise of invading armies.
- **"Wail, O dwellers of the Hollow"** – "Maktesh" (the Mortar/Hollow) was probably the market district in the Tyropoeon Valley, a depressed area shaped like a mortar. Bridgeway Commentary identifies it as "the market area in the lower part of the city" (studylight.org/bbc).
- **"All your merchants will be silenced; all who weigh out silver will be cut off"** – God's judgment targets those who trust in commerce and wealth. Guzik: "Merchants and those with money trusted in their riches, and now God promises to cut down those steeped in that kind of idolatry" (enduringword.com).
- **Source URLs**: enduringword.com, studylight.org/bbc

---

### vv. 12–13 – Judgment on the Complacent

- **"I will search Jerusalem with lamps"** – A vivid image: no one will escape, no hiding place will work. Guzik cites Baker: "Unlike Diogenes, the pre-Christian Greek philosopher who was searching for an honest man, Yahweh in this context does not seek righteousness but sin to punish and eradicate" (enduringword.com).
- **"The men settled in complacency"** – Literally "settled on their lees" (KJV), an image from winemaking: wine left too long on its sediment becomes thick and syrupy, a picture of spiritual stagnation. Peake's Commentary describes them as "the morally indifferent who are settled on their lees" (studylight.org/peake).
- **"Who say to themselves, 'The LORD will do nothing, either good or bad'"** – Practical deism or practical atheism: the belief that God is distant and uninvolved. Guzik compares this to the "clockmaker" god of Deism who winds up the universe and leaves it ticking. He quotes Edward Gibbon's description of late Roman attitudes: people regarded all religions as equally true, philosophers as equally false, and politicians as equally useful (enduringword.com). Gill: these men "lived without God in the world, and as if there was no God" (biblehub.com/gill).
- **"They will build houses but not inhabit them"** – A covenant curse from Deuteronomy 28:30, 39, now applied to the complacent wealthy.
- **Source URLs**: enduringword.com, biblehub.com/gill, studylight.org/peake

---

### v. 14 – The Great Day of the LORD Is Near

- **"The great Day of the LORD is near—near and coming quickly"** – The repetition emphasises imminence. Guzik: "The term 'day of the LORD' (used more than 25 times in the Bible) does not necessarily refer to one specific day; it speaks of 'God's time.'" Now is the day of man, but one day the Messiah will end the day of man (enduringword.com). The Layman's Bible Commentary emphasises the suddenness and imminence (studylight.org/lbc).
- **"The cry of the mighty will be bitter"** – Even the warriors will weep in terror. Precept Austin notes this begins a section describing the intensity of divine judgment (preceptaustin.org).
- **Source URLs**: enduringword.com, studylight.org/lbc, preceptaustin.org

---

### vv. 15–16 – The Character of That Day

- **"A day of wrath… trouble and distress… destruction and desolation… darkness and gloom… clouds and blackness"** – A torrent of paired synonyms. Precept Austin explains: "The joining of synonyms in this way emphasizes the degree of the characteristic being described. The first two pairs focus on the distress and ruin that judgment will bring; the second two pairs picture this day of judgment as being very dark (darkness) and exceedingly overcast (gloom)" (preceptaustin.org).
- **Dies Irae connection**: Guzik notes that the Vulgate translation of this passage ("Dies irae, dies illa") became the opening line of the famous medieval requiem sequence *Dies Irae*, attributed to Thomas of Celano (enduringword.com). The Expositor's Bible Commentary observes: "It was with a true instinct that the great Christian singer of the Last Day took from Zephaniah his keynote" (studylight.org/teb).
- **"A day of horn blast and battle cry against the fortified cities, and against the high corner towers"** – Military imagery: the shofar (ram's horn) alarm and the shouts of attackers. Fortified cities and high towers (human defences) will offer no protection. Precept Austin notes this concludes the description of the Day with "two familiar battle sounds" (preceptaustin.org).
- **Source URLs**: enduringword.com, preceptaustin.org, studylight.org/teb

---

### v. 17 – Distress, Blindness, and Blood

- **"I will bring such distress on mankind that they will walk like the blind"** – Utter helplessness and disorientation in the face of judgment. Precept Austin (citing Deffinbaugh): "The former leaders and other influential persons will find that they are as helpless and defenceless as the blind and the poor whom they have exploited" (preceptaustin.org; studylight.org/bbc).
- **"Because they have sinned against the LORD"** – The cause is explicitly stated: sin against Yahweh. Guzik: "God wants to make it plain and certain that He will judge a rebellious Judah" (enduringword.com).
- **"Their blood will be poured out like dust and their flesh like dung"** – Graphic imagery of total contempt for human life in the day of wrath; corpses treated as worthless refuse. The Layman's Bible Commentary says "flesh is exposed and left to rot upon the ground" (studylight.org/lbc).
- **Source URLs**: enduringword.com, preceptaustin.org, studylight.org/lbc, studylight.org/bbc

---

### v. 18 – Neither Silver Nor Gold Will Deliver

- **"Neither their silver nor their gold will be able to deliver them"** – Wealth is useless against divine wrath. Guzik: "Men trust in silver and gold, but it will do them no good on the day of God's judgment" (enduringword.com). Peake's Commentary: "no silver or gold shall be able to deliver them from the flame of His jealousy" (studylight.org/peake).
- **"The whole earth will be consumed by the fire of His jealousy"** – God's jealousy is His passionate commitment to His own honour and to the welfare of His beloved. Ray Stedman (cited at Precept Austin): "God loves so thoroughly, so completely, that he cannot brook a rival to his love. God will destroy anything which hurts his loved one" (preceptaustin.org). Precept Austin notes that v. 18 broadens from the historical judgment on Judah to encompass "all the inhabitants of the world," pointing to the eschatological fulfillment (preceptaustin.org).
- **"He will make a sudden end of all who dwell on the earth"** – Literally "a speedy riddance" (KJV). The judgment, when it comes, will be swift and complete. Gill notes this final verse shows the inevitability of the judgment — nothing can deliver from it (biblehub.com/gill).
- **Source URLs**: enduringword.com, preceptaustin.org, biblehub.com/gill, studylight.org/peake

## Denominational Perspectives and Other Views

**Note**: Due to tool limits, I could not fetch full pages from most denominational sources. What follows is based on fragmentary search results and general knowledge derivable from the sources accessed.

### Reformed / Presbyterian
- The theme of God's absolute sovereignty in judgment runs through Reformed readings. Keil & Delitzsch (accessed via studylight.org) emphasise the universality of judgment — it falls on "all the world" (vv. 2–3), then on Judah specifically (vv. 4–7), then on "sinners of every rank" (vv. 8–13), and then "irresistibly upon all the inhabitants of the earth" (vv. 14–18) (studylight.org/kdo). Precept Austin draws heavily on Walter Kaiser (a prominent evangelical OT scholar in the Reformed tradition), who structures the chapter as a unified announcement of the Day of the Lord (preceptaustin.org).

### Baptist
- **John Gill** (biblehub.com/gill) provides a thorough Baptist perspective, emphasising particular atonement language: in v. 7 the Jewish people become "a sacrifice to his justice, to atone in some measure for the injury done to it by their sins." He also applies v. 5's syncretists to "all such persons that seek for justification and salvation, partly by their own works, and partly by Christ." Gill represents a classic Particular Baptist covenantal reading (biblehub.com/gill).

### Pentecostal / Charismatic
- **David Guzik** (enduringword.com) represents a broadly charismatic/evangelical reading. He emphasises the prophetic as "invitation" — God's judgment announcement is simultaneously a call to repent (enduringword.com). Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel, via studylight.org/smith) sees a "double aspect of fulfillment" with both the Babylonian destruction and the Great Tribulation in view. Precept Austin includes Ray Stedman (a well-known evangelical expositor), who treats the Day of the Lord as both historical and future (preceptaustin.org).

The Vulgate's translation of v. 15 (*Dies irae, dies illa*) formed the basis of the medieval requiem sequence, noted by Guzik (enduringword.com) and Walker (cited in enduringword.com). This is a significant point of Catholic liturgical heritage.

### Modern Scholarship
- **Precept Austin** cites the NET Bible notes on the origin of "the Day of the LORD" concept: "It may have originated in the ancient Near Eastern idea of the sovereign's day of conquest, where a king would boast that he had concluded an entire military campaign in a single day" (citing D. Stuart, BASOR 221 [1976]) (preceptaustin.org).
- The **Expositor's Bible Commentary** (studylight.org/teb) makes an important observation about Zephaniah's place in the development of prophecy: "With Zephaniah the Day of the Lord tends to become the Last Day. His book is the first tinging of prophecy with apocalypse: that is the moment which it supplies in the history of Israel's religion" (studylight.org/teb).
- **Bridgeway Commentary** (studylight.org/bbc) provides a non-denominational evangelical reading, identifying the Scythians or Babylonians as the human instruments (studylight.org/bbc).
- **Peake's Commentary** (studylight.org/peake) is a classic modern critical commentary, and it identifies the "guests" in v. 7 specifically as the Scythians (studylight.org/peake).

### Points of Interpretive Tension Between Traditions

1. **The identity of the "guests" (v. 7)**: Gill sees the Chaldeans as the primary guests, with birds and beasts also invited (biblehub.com/gill). Peake identifies Scythians (studylight.org/peake). The Pulpit Commentary is non-specific: "the particular agents intended are not specified by the prophet, whose mission was not directed to any such definition" (biblehub.com/pulpit, via search).

2. **"The stumbling blocks" (v. 3)**: The Hebrew is ambiguous. Some (Gill, Guzik, KJV) render it as idols that cause stumbling. Others (ESV, NIV) translate it as "rubble" or "ruins," reflecting a different textual judgement. Precept Austin catalogues the various translations without adjudicating (preceptaustin.org).

3. **Scope of judgment**: Gill and the Pulpit Commentary tend to read "the land" (v. 2) as specifically the land of Judah, while Guzik and Precept Austin see a deliberate oscillation between local (Judah) and universal (the whole earth / eschatological) judgment — a "near and far" duality (enduringword.com; preceptaustin.org). This affects how one reads the chapter's relationship to end-times prophecy.

4. **Dating relative to Josiah's reform**: Gill discusses the question at length — if Zephaniah prophesied before the reform, the "remnant of Baal" (v. 4) refers to what remained after the northern kingdom's exile; if after, it refers to what Josiah's reform left untouched. Most commentators (MacArthur, Guzik, Precept Austin sources) favour an early date (pre-reform, c. 635–625 BC) (biblehub.com/gill; preceptaustin.org; enduringword.com).
